ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The PREVENT-AD study was approved by the institutional review boards of McGill University and the Douglas Mental Health University Institute.
The UCLouvain study was approved by the Ethics Committee of UCLouvain (UCL-2016-121, Date: 13/05/2019; Eudra-CT number: 2018-0034/73-94; 2010/17May/148).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Participants completed olfactory testing, underwent tau-PET imaging, and structural MRI.
Results: CN A+ participants had significantly lower odor identification performance than CN A-participants, with no evidence of cohort heterogeneity.

At enrollment, participants completed a health review, neurological and physical examination, blood sampling, structural MRI, and cognitive assessment including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 30, and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) 31 .
table.formatted: At enrollment, participants completed a health review, neurological and physical examination, blood sampling, structural MRI, and cognitive assessment including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 30 , and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">31</ref> .

table.text: Participants were excluded if clinical consensus determined probable MCI, major neurological or psychiatric illness, substance abuse, or contraindications to MRI or lumbar puncture.
Amyloid status was determined using [ 18 F]NAV4694 PET and quantified on the Centiloid scale; participants were considered amyloid-positive when the Centiloid value exceeded 20 34 .
From the PREVENT-AD cohort, 159 CN A-and 58 CN A+ participants were included.
Older adult participants were enrolled in a study conducted at UCLouvain, Brussels, Belgium.

Patients were recruited through the memory clinic of the Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc, whereas volunteers were recruited from ongoing research studies and through mailbox announcements distributed in the hospital's neighborhood.

Thirty-eight participants were drawn from the UCL-2018-0034/73-94 study, with data collected between March 2019 and January 2025, and the remaining participants were drawn from the UCL-2011-001756-12 study, with data collected between 2012 and 2021.

Exclusion criteria for both patients and volunteers included focal brain lesions, epileptic seizures, major depression or psychiatric conditions, alcohol or drug abuse, chronic rhinosinusitis, and head trauma.
Eligible participants were ≥60 years old or 55-59 years old if ≤15 years of the youngest age at onset in their affected first-degree relative.

Participants had at least six years of education, were fluent in French and/or English, had a study partner, and Participants underwent a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment, amyloid PET imaging or spinal tap, and structural MRI.
Participants were excluded if they were classified as having MCI, with at least one cognitive domain impaired.
In total, 40 CN participants were included in the primary cross-sectional group comparisons and 34 had longitudinal follow-up available for the incident-MCI analyses.
In total, 257 participants were included, comprising 181 CN A-and 76 CN A+.
In PREVENT-AD, CN A+ participants had lower unadjusted UPSIT scores than CN A-participants (p = .027), whereas demographic variables did not differ by amyloid status.
In UCLouvain, CN A+ participants were older (p = .025) and had lower MMSE scores (p = .022) than CN A-participants; Sniffin' Sticks scores did not differ significantly by amyloid status.
Among UCLouvain participants, visually assessed tau-positive (T+; n = 11) participants had lower mean odor identification scores than tau-negative (T-; n = 20) participants (56.2% vs 73.4%).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

live_data_statements: Participants completed olfactory testing, underwent tau-PET imaging, and structural MRI.
Results: CN A+ participants had significantly lower odor identification performance than CN A-participants, with no evidence of cohort heterogeneity.

At enrollment, participants completed a health review, neurological and physical examination, blood sampling, structural MRI, and cognitive assessment including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 30, and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) 31 .
Participants were excluded if clinical consensus determined probable MCI, major neurological or psychiatric illness, substance abuse, or contraindications to MRI or lumbar puncture.
Amyloid status was determined using [ 18 F]NAV4694 PET and quantified on the Centiloid scale; participants were considered amyloid-positive when the Centiloid value exceeded 20 34 .
From the PREVENT-AD cohort, 159 CN A-and 58 CN A+ participants were included.
Older adult participants were enrolled in a study conducted at UCLouvain, Brussels, Belgium.

Patients were recruited through the memory clinic of the Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc, whereas volunteers were recruited from ongoing research studies and through mailbox announcements distributed in the hospital's neighborhood.

Thirty-eight participants were drawn from the UCL-2018-0034/73-94 study, with data collected between March 2019 and January 2025, and the remaining participants were drawn from the UCL-2011-001756-12 study, with data collected between 2012 and 2021.

Exclusion criteria for both patients and volunteers included focal brain lesions, epileptic seizures, major depression or psychiatric conditions, alcohol or drug abuse, chronic rhinosinusitis, and head trauma.
Eligible participants were ≥60 years old or 55-59 years old if ≤15 years of the youngest age at onset in their affected first-degree relative.

Participants had at least six years of education, were fluent in French and/or English, had a study partner, and Participants underwent a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment, amyloid PET imaging or spinal tap, and structural MRI.
Participants were excluded if they were classified as having MCI, with at least one cognitive domain impaired.
In total, 40 CN participants were included in the primary cross-sectional group comparisons and 34 had longitudinal follow-up available for the incident-MCI analyses.
In total, 257 participants were included, comprising 181 CN A-and 76 CN A+.
In PREVENT-AD, CN A+ participants had lower unadjusted UPSIT scores than CN A-participants (p = .027), whereas demographic variables did not differ by amyloid status.
In UCLouvain, CN A+ participants were older (p = .025) and had lower MMSE scores (p = .022) than CN A-participants; Sniffin' Sticks scores did not differ significantly by amyloid status.
Among UCLouvain participants, visually assessed tau-positive (T+; n = 11) participants had lower mean odor identification scores than tau-negative (T-; n = 20) participants (56.2% vs 73.4%).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
